lesson.title: Chains Within Chains: Differentiating Triple Compositions
lesson.summary: When three or more functions are nested inside one another, the chain rule applies repeatedly from the outside in, multiplying one derivative factor at each layer.
lesson.body:
Some expressions nest more than two functions together, such as sin((x^2+1)^3) or sqrt(ln(5x)). These are compositions of three functions rather than two, and the nested chain rule extends the same outside-times-inside logic one more layer: differentiate the outermost function first, multiply by the derivative of the middle function, then multiply again by the derivative of the innermost function. Every layer contributes exactly one multiplicative factor, and no layer can be skipped without losing part of the true rate of change.

For h(x) = f(g(k(x))), the multiple chain rule states h'(x) = f'(g(k(x))) times g'(k(x)) times k'(x). Each factor is evaluated at the appropriate stage: f' is evaluated at g(k(x)), the output of the two inner functions together, while g' is evaluated only at k(x), and k' is evaluated at plain x. This is simply the nested chain rule applied twice in a row, once to peel off the outermost layer and once more to peel off the middle layer, and it relies on the same f'(g(x))g'(x) pattern from the composition derivative rule at every stage.

Differentiate y = sin((x^2+1)^3). Identify the three layers from outside in: sine is outermost, then cubing, then x^2+1 is innermost. Let w = x^2+1, v = w^3, y = sin(v). Then dy/dv = cos(v) = cos((x^2+1)^3). dv/dw = 3w^2 = 3(x^2+1)^2. dw/dx = 2x. Multiplying all three: dy/dx = cos((x^2+1)^3) times 3(x^2+1)^2 times 2x = 6x(x^2+1)^2 cos((x^2+1)^3). Check by grouping differently: treat u = (x^2+1)^3 as a single inside function for sine, so dy/dx = cos(u) times du/dx, and compute du/dx using the power chain rule directly: du/dx = 3(x^2+1)^2 times 2x = 6x(x^2+1)^2. Multiplying by cos(u) gives the identical result, confirming the answer two different ways.

The two ways of grouping the problem above, three separate layers versus combining the inner two layers into one power chain rule step, are both valid and always agree, because the chain rule is associative: it does not matter whether you peel one layer at a time or combine several inner layers first, as long as every derivative factor from the innermost function outward eventually gets multiplied in exactly once. This flexibility is genuinely useful, since some problems are easier to organize as two layers with one layer pre-combined, while others are clearer written out fully as three or more separate steps.

The main practical challenge with multiple chain rule problems is bookkeeping rather than new concepts, keeping track of which expression each derivative should be evaluated at and making sure no layer gets skipped or duplicated. Writing out each intermediate variable explicitly, as w, v, and y above, is a reliable way to avoid dropping a factor, and this same layering habit carries directly into more advanced nested derivative problems later in a calculus sequence, including the multiple chain rule extension of this exact idea to even longer chains of composed functions.
